messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 61
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Paramedic
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 35

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Workplace: Workplace, Darkness: Dark spaces, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Prevention: ruminate about how event could have been prevented, Constant Socialising: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ravi Shah was a 61-year-old South Asian man who had spent most of his adult life working as a paramedic, a role he had long regarded with pride and discipline. He was married, well known in his family for being dependable, and still living with the practical routines that had shaped his work for decades. The event he described had occurred on a shift that was supposed to be ordinary, when he and a colleague were called to a scene involving a toxic chemical exposure. Ravi did not dwell on the technical details unless asked, but he was clear that the smell of alcohol in the air had been part of the moment, sharp and unmistakable, and that it had become fixed in his mind as the scene developed. The call had taken him into a workplace environment that, for him now, could feel uncomfortably similar to the site of that exposure: any return to a workplace setting could bring back the same uneasy alertness, as if the present had suddenly become the past.

Since that day, Ravi had found himself reacting to dark spaces in a way he had not before. He did not describe ordinary nighttime as the issue, but rather those enclosed or poorly lit spaces where he could not immediately take in what was around him. In those moments, his body would tense and his mind would begin to search for the chemical incident before he had even consciously named it. He spoke about how certain smells could do the same thing, and the alcohol odor was the one that most reliably unsettled him. It was not simply unpleasant; it was a cue that carried him back with startling force. He could be moving through an ordinary day and then, without warning, something in his surroundings would bring the full memory back. When that happened, he said, it was not like thinking about something that had happened in the past. It was more like being dropped into it again.

What made the memory so difficult for him was not only that it arrived suddenly, but that it came with the same terror he had felt at the time. Ravi described moments when the recollection would hit with such intensity that he had to stop whatever he was doing. He would go quiet, put down what was in his hands, and wait for the wave of feeling to pass. He did not speak about the memory as a distant story; instead, he said that when it returned, the fear was immediate and overwhelming, as if his mind and body had not learned that the danger was over. He had come to fear the memory itself, knowing that once it surfaced he might not be able to carry on with the conversation or task in front of him.

Over the months after the event, Ravi began making choices that narrowed his world in ways that he initially saw as practical. He found himself avoiding hospitals, ambulances, and physical examinations whenever he could. Those settings carried too many reminders of the incident and of his work as a paramedic, and he preferred to stay away from them rather than risk being flooded by the memory. Even when he needed medical care, he would delay or look for reasons to put it off. In daily life, he also tried to keep himself constantly surrounded by people so he was never alone with his thoughts. He described this not as social enjoyment, though he valued his family and company, but as a deliberate effort to avoid the long stretches of quiet in which his mind might turn back toward the exposure. He arranged his time so that there was always someone around, whether at home, with relatives, or in other company, because solitude made him uneasy.

He also spent a great deal of time ruminating about how the event could have been prevented. Ravi’s mind repeatedly returned to the details of the call, going over what he could have noticed sooner, what steps might have changed the outcome, and where the sequence might have been interrupted. He knew this did not change what had happened, but he felt driven to review it anyway, as though if he could find the exact point where things went wrong, he might make sense of why it had happened at all. These reflections were rarely comforting; they tended to leave him more preoccupied and drained. Still, he found it hard to stop himself, and the effort of checking and rechecking the past became part of his private routine.

By the time he sought help, Ravi was exhausted by the way the memory could still seize him, by the fear that came back full force, and by the amount of organizing his life now required to keep himself away from reminders. He had not come to therapy because he thought the event was behind him; he came because it remained too present. He was most afraid that another sudden reminder would hit him when he was alone or unprepared, leaving him overwhelmed by the same terror all over again. At the same time, he hoped that with help he might finally be able to face the memory without having to stop in his tracks, and to move through his work and home life without needing to guard himself so constantly against what might suddenly return.
